bibliographic.title: Trustworthy Generative AI for Financial Services
bibliographic.authors: Marc-André Zöller; Anastasiia Iurshina; Ines Röder
bibliographic.venue: Symposium on Scaling AI Assessments (SAIA 2024), OASIcs
bibliographic.citation_apa: Zöller, M.-A., Iurshina, A., & Röder, I. (2024). Trustworthy generative AI for financial services. In Symposium on Scaling AI Assessments (SAIA 2024). https://doi.org/10.4230/OASIcs.SAIA.2024.2

methodology.method_family: practitioner platform architecture and solution description
methodology.study_design: practitioner track solution architecture with illustrative deployment in a financial institution
methodology.sample_description: demonstration within a large-scale financial institution; no detailed participant or dataset description in provided text
methodology.technology_context: GFT EnterpriseGPT platform using LLM providers (local open-source or commercial), with guardrails, privacy-preserving techniques, grounding/context augmentation, document search, API queries, and GFT AI Shield

eligibility.decision_rationale: The paper directly addresses trustworthy GenAI governance for regulated financial services through guardrails, privacy, grounding, compliance, and audit-related use cases, but the provided text does not substantively address conversational systems, chatbots, or conversational governance mechanisms.
eligibility.manual_spotcheck_reason: Conversational relevance is absent in the extracted evidence while governance and regulated-domain relevance are strong; full-text sections beyond the excerpt should be checked for customer-support or dialogue-specific governance content.

appraisal.notes: Practitioner-track architecture paper with clear safeguard categories, but limited transparent empirical evaluation, sample detail, and limitations discussion in the provided text.

cerqual.explanation: The safeguard framework is internally coherent and relevant to regulated LLM governance, but outcome claims are weakly supported in the provided text and conversational governance is not evidenced.

coding.theme: Trustworthy GenAI governance for regulated financial services
coding.subtheme: Multi-level platform safeguards via guardrails, privacy, and grounding

synthesis.main_claim: GFT EnterpriseGPT enables regulatory-compliant, trustworthy GenAI in financial services through multi-level safeguards combining guardrails, privacy-preserving techniques, and grounding mechanisms.
synthesis.contribution: Describes a practitioner platform architecture and workflow for safely deploying LLM-based GenAI in finance, including input/output guardrails, local privacy inspection, and context augmentation before LLM processing.
synthesis.limitations: Provided text offers limited empirical detail on evaluation design, sample size, measured outcomes, and limitations; conversational governance is not developed.
synthesis.use_in_review: Use as supporting evidence on technical and compliance-oriented GenAI governance in regulated finance, especially guardrails, privacy controls, grounding/RAG-like augmentation, and audit/compliance applications; not central for conversational governance.

evidence.claim: Paper introduces a regulatory-compliant trustworthy GenAI platform for financial services
evidence.excerpt: This work introduces GFT EnterpriseGPT, a regulatory-compliant, trustworthy generative AI (GenAI) platform tailored for the financial services sector.

evidence.claim: Governance approach combines guardrails, privacy, and grounding
evidence.excerpt: Our solution addresses these challenges through multi-level safeguards, including robust guardrails, privacy-preserving techniques, and grounding mechanisms.

evidence.claim: Deployment demonstrated in a large financial institution with claimed efficiency and compliance gains
evidence.excerpt: We demonstrate the practical application of GFT EnterpriseGPT within a large-scale financial institution, where it successfully improves operational efficiency and compliance.

evidence.claim: Regulated financial domain with compliance and audit use cases
evidence.excerpt: In the financial sector data privacy, ethical considerations, and regulatory compliance are paramount.

evidence.claim: GenAI positioned for audit assistance and regulatory compliance support
evidence.excerpt: GenAI can be used in the compliance office to optimize processes and to increase efficiency.

evidence.claim: Audit-assistant functions include policy overview, change detection, conflict detection, and gap identification
evidence.excerpt: As an auditing assistant, GenAI can provide comprehensive overviews of existing rules and policies, highlight changes from previous versions, detect conflicting policies, and ensure alignment with internal guidelines.

evidence.claim: Platform uses LLM providers with context augmentation workflow
evidence.excerpt: Finally, the augmented prompt is forwarded to an large language model (LLM) provider, e.g., a local open-source model or a commercial provider.

evidence.claim: Trustworthy measures organized into guardrails, privacy, and grounding
evidence.excerpt: In general, these measures fall into three categor- ies: guardrails, privacy and grounding.

evidence.claim: Input and output guardrails mitigate risk and check hallucinations
evidence.excerpt: Input guardrails verify that requests that are classified as risky will not enter the LLM model

evidence.claim: Provider safety measures alone are insufficient for specific regulated use cases
evidence.excerpt: While this provides a solid basis for ethical GenAI, they are not sufficient in practice as they can not be adapted to specific use cases and can be overcome by malicious actors [3].

evidence.claim: Privacy shield prevents forwarding sensitive prompts to commercial providers
evidence.excerpt: Only when no violations, for example, a prompt containing credit card information, were detected, the user prompt is forwarded to an LLM for answer generation.

evidence.claim: Local inspection methods include pattern matching and named-entity recognition
evidence.excerpt: Simple pattern matching is used to detect restricted words Named-entity recognition [13] using a local neural network checks if restricted categories are used in the

evidence.claim: Flagged prompts are blocked with user notification
evidence.excerpt: If a prompt is flagged by one of the filters, the user is informed why the request is not being processed.

evidence.claim: Customer support is mentioned only as a possible application, not as the study focus
evidence.excerpt: particularly in applications such as credit assessments [4], personalized financial advice [6], customer support [2], investment research [6], or audit assistance for regulatory compli- ance [12].

evidence.claim: Transparency and trust are explicit goals of the safeguard design
evidence.excerpt: ensuring reliability, transparency, and adherence to ethical and regulatory standards.
